query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW, the introduction of a minor amount (~0.1 at.%) of boron followed by a controlled high-temperature annealing treatment will induce the formation of finely dispersed intergranular boride precipitates. This modification is expected to enhance grain-boundary cohesion, thereby significantly improving room-temperature ductility (e.g., increasing compressive or tensile ductility from ~2% to >10%) while preserving the high-temperature strength (retaining excellent yield properties up to 1600 °C) and simultaneously providing additional defect sinks that mitigate helium bubble formation during irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with poor room-temperature ductility but excellent high-temperature strength.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.1 at.% boron into the NbMoTaW alloy composition during melting and alloying, then apply a controlled thermal annealing treatment (e.g., annealing at a temperature sufficiently high to allow intergranular boride nucleation but below temperatures that risk phase instability) to promote precipitation at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical testing to assess ductility, high-temperature mechanical performance testing up to 1600 °C, and helium ion irradiation experiments (at reactor-relevant fluences and temperatures, e.g., around 900–1050 K) to evaluate irradiation-induced defect evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely dispersed, nanoscale boride precipitates localized preferentially at grain boundaries within the continuous BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The boride precipitates enhance grain-boundary cohesion and act as effective sinks for irradiation-induced defects such as He bubbles. This leads to an improved transition from intergranular to transgranular fracture, boosting room-temperature ductility while the continuous BCC matrix maintains high-temperature mechanical strength and structural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the boron-modified alloy will exhibit a significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (quantitatively, an expected increase in fracture strain from roughly 2% to over 10%), retain comparable high yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., minimal degradation of strength at 1600 °C), and display reduced irradiation-induced blistering and precipitation due to enhanced defect recombination and trapping at the boride interfaces.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy which has excellent high-temperature performance but shows limited ductility at room temperature and only computationally inferred irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: The intervention should maintain phase stability of the BCC structure across the operational temperature range (room temperature up to 1600 °C) and under irradiation doses relevant to reactor conditions (e.g., several dpa with He implantation up to ~8–10% He concentration) without triggering deleterious amorphization or excessive precipitate coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact nucleation kinetics and distribution of the boride precipitates, their long-term thermal stability at 1600 °C, and potential interactions with irradiation-induced defects. Additionally, the scalability of the precise boron doping level and annealing protocol to industrial scales warrants investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of NbMoTaW alloy samples: one set with 0.1 at.% boron added and processed via the specified thermal annealing protocol, and a control set without boron. Perform comprehensive mechanical testing at room temperature and high temperatures (up to 1600 °C), and subject both sets to standardized helium ion irradiation experiments at elevated temperature (e.g., 900–1050 K). Characterize the microstructure using TEM and APT to evaluate the presence and distribution of intergranular boride precipitates.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile or compressive ductility (fracture strain)
High-temperature yield strength and phase stability (XRD, TEM)
Irradiation-induced defect evolution (He bubble density and size via TEM/APT)
Fractography to assess the transition from intergranular to transgranular failure modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility, do not maintain comparable high-temperature strength and phase stability, or if the irradiation experiments reveal no reduction in defect formation (or even exacerbate irradiation-induced damage compared to the control), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. While pure W may have the most ideal combination of the He bubble size and density of the materials studied here, there are significant concerns for the usage of W in a fission or fusion reactor, including its ductile–brittle transition temperature, recrystallization, and the ability to fabricate complex components. The performance of additively manufactured RHEAs in other areas relevant for reactors, including fracture properties and recrystallization performance, must be explored further. Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Helium irradiation and He bubble formation and accumulation is just one aspect of materials design that should motivate materials choices for future reactors. In this work, we show that compositionally complex (spanning two, three, and four-component alloys) can be developed with AM processing routes. Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

papers.title: Compositional Effects of Additively Manufactured Refractory High-Entropy Alloys under High-Energy Helium Irradiation.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) based on W, Ta, Cr, V (2–4 component systems) processed by additive manufacturing
papers.approach: Utilized AM processing to produce complex, compositionally diverse HEAs and then exposed them to high-energy He ion irradiation
papers.findings: Enhanced compositional complexity tends to improve irradiation tolerance by reducing He bubble accumulation; homogeneous microstructures free of segregation yield the best performance under irradiation
papers.mechanism: Mitigation occurs via engineered microstructures that trap He bubbles at interfaces/precipitates and promote defect recombination

papers.title: A quinary WTaCrVHf nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy withholding extreme irradiation environments.
papers.system: Quinary alloy in the W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf system forming a single-phase BCC microstructure in both thin-film and bulk forms
papers.approach: Combined in situ irradiation experiments (He implantation and dual-beam heavy ion irradiation) with simulation to assess thermal stability and defect evolution
papers.findings: The alloy retains a stable BCC structure with minimal dislocation loop formation and exhibits grain size refinement under dual-beam irradiation; irradiation-induced cavity formation saturates at moderate doses
papers.mechanism: Irradiation cascades promote self-healing through grain refinement while the nanocrystalline structure limits defect growth

papers.title: Outstanding radiation resistance of tungsten-based high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: W-based refractory HEA (W–Ta–Cr–V) grown as thin films with bimodal grain sizes (nanocrystalline and ultrafine regimes)
papers.approach: Magnetron sputtering deposition followed by irradiation at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 1073 K) with He and heavy ions
papers.findings: The material develops Cr–V-rich precipitates in the matrix under irradiation without forming dislocation loops; exhibits negligible irradiation hardening despite high doses
papers.mechanism: Enhanced point defect recombination and the formation of secondary Cr–V phases (likely serving as defect sinks) contribute to its exceptional radiation resistance

papers.title: Microstructural Design for Improving Ductility of An Initially Brittle Refractory High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Refractory HEA based on systems including Al, Nb, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr exhibiting an initial two‐phase (ordered B2 + BCC) microstructure
papers.approach: Applied controlled thermal treatments and slow cooling to invert the microstructure from a continuous, brittle B2 matrix to a continuous, ductile disordered BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates
papers.findings: Microstructure inversion dramatically improves room-temperature compressive ductility (exceeding 20%) while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperatures
papers.mechanism: The phase inversion reduces the proportion of the brittle ordered phase and leverages precipitation strengthening in a ductile BCC matrix

papers.title: High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Refractory HEA composed of Nb, Ta, Hf, Ti, Zr, and V0.5
papers.approach: Tensile tests conducted from room temperature to 1273 K combined with TEM observations to elucidate the deformation mechanisms
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits high yield strength and good ductility at room temperature (12% ductility at 473 K) while maintaining yield strengths above 800 MPa in the intermediate temperature range
papers.mechanism: Plastic deformation is governed by dislocation slip with the density of dislocations closely correlating to the observed strength and ductility

papers.title: He-ion Irradiation Effects on the Microstructures and Mechanical Properties of the Ti-Zr-Hf-V-Ta Low-Activation High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Low-activation HEAs in the Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 family with a single-phase BCC structure
papers.approach: He-ion irradiation at elevated temperature (1023 K) with subsequent analysis of microstructural stability and mechanical properties
papers.findings: The alloys remain as single-phase BCC with no apparent radiation-induced segregation or precipitation; moderate irradiation hardening is observed with cavity size and density increasing with fluence
papers.mechanism: Enhanced radiation tolerance arises from the low solubility of He and slow diffusion of point defects in the BCC matrix

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA with a minor addition (0.1 at.%) of boron
papers.approach: Introduced a trace element (boron) to induce controlled intergranular precipitation of HCP borides (likely (Hf, Zr)B2) and conducted mechanical testing
papers.findings: Boron addition leads to intergranular boride formation, markedly enhancing grain-boundary cohesion, work hardenability, and ductility (transition from intergranular to transgranular fracture modes)
papers.mechanism: The precipitated borides at grain boundaries act to strengthen and toughen the interface without significant embrittlement of the matrix

established: BCC-structured refractory HEAs provide excellent high-temperature strength but often suffer from poor room-temperature ductility and face irradiation-induced defect challenges.
Enhanced compositional complexity and homogeneous microstructure formation can improve irradiation resistance, particularly under helium implantation conditions.
Microstructural engineering—such as phase inversion or tailored precipitation—has been shown to effectively improve room-temperature ductility while preserving high-temperature performance.

approaches_tried.approach: Increasing compositional entropy via additive manufacturing to yield homogeneous microstructures
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved irradiation tolerance with reduced He bubble growth and blistering

approaches_tried.approach: Developing quinary alloys by adding elements such as Hf to the base WMoTaW system
approaches_tried.outcome: Stable single-phase BCC structure with enhanced irradiation resistance (minimal dislocation loops and controlled cavity formation)

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal treatment to induce microstructural phase inversion (from continuous ordered B2 to continuous disordered BCC)
approaches_tried.outcome: Significant improvement in room-temperature ductility while retaining high strength at elevated temperatures

approaches_tried.approach: Minor alloying (e.g., boron addition) to promote intergranular boride precipitation
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion leading to improved work hardenability and ductility

mechanisms: Trapping of He bubbles at engineered interfaces or secondary precipitates, reducing irradiation-induced swelling
Enhanced solute–dislocation interactions (including edge dislocation control) that contribute to high strength retention
Phase inversion or transformation-induced plasticity that increases ductility by switching the dominant phase from brittle to ductile
Intergranular precipitation (e.g., boride formation) that reinforces grain-boundary cohesion
disagreements: Some studies report that certain alloying elements (e.g., V) may be detrimental under He irradiation, while others find benefits from compositional complexity
Differences exist in the interpretation of irradiation-induced features – whether observed nanoscale features are dislocation loops or secondary-phase precipitates
open_questions: What is the optimal balance of alloying elements in a NbMoTaW-derived system to simultaneously achieve high-temperature strength, improved room-temperature ductility, and irradiation resistance?
How do minor additions (e.g., boron) and controlled phase transformations interact during prolonged exposure to reactor-relevant irradiation and thermal environments?
What are the long-term stability and evolution of the dual-phase microstructures under combined high-temperature and irradiation stress?
opportunities: Investigate a combined intervention that integrates microstructural phase inversion (to form a continuous ductile BCC matrix with discrete strengthening precipitates) and minor alloying (e.g., boron addition) to enhance grain-boundary cohesion in NbMoTaW-based alloys
Explore processing routes (such as additive manufacturing with rapid cooling) that enable grain refinement and homogeneous elemental distribution to suppress irradiation-induced damage

Perform systematic studies on the effect of tailored thermal annealing and alloying modifications (e.g., controlled Hf or boron content) in single-phase BCC RHEAs to optimize the trade-offs between room-temperature ductility and high-temperature performance

directions.direction: Minor alloying addition of boron to promote intergranular boride precipitation
directions.assessment: Adding a trace amount (~0.1 at.%) of boron has been shown in similar refractory HEAs to induce the formation of intergranular boride precipitates that enhance grain‐boundary cohesion and shift the fracture mode from intergranular to transgranular. This approach directly targets poor room‐temperature ductility while minimally affecting the single-phase BCC matrix that imparts high-temperature strength. The mechanism is supported by evidence (e.g., PMC9572892) and is feasible through controlled alloy synthesis and thermal processing.

directions.direction: Controlled thermal annealing to induce phase inversion
directions.assessment: Thermal treatments that invert the microstructure (e.g., transforming a continuous brittle ordered phase into a disordered ductile BCC matrix with discrete precipitates) have been shown to improve ductility (PMC5995863). While this route improves room-temperature performance, it must be carefully controlled so that the high-temperature BCC phase stability is preserved. It may be more challenging to maintain the irradiation tolerance if the precipitates evolve adversely under neutron/He irradiation.

directions.direction: Optimized compositional modifications by minor additions of elements such as Hf
directions.assessment: Introducing a small amount of elements like Hf to the NbMoTaW base could tailor lattice distortion to improve ductility and also influence defect dynamics under irradiation, as seen in related W-based HEAs (PMC10154406). However, recent work indicates that such additions require tight control to avoid detrimental precipitation at reactor‐relevant temperatures.

directions.direction: Process control via additive manufacturing for grain refinement
directions.assessment: Rapid solidification through additive manufacturing offers a route to obtain a homogeneous, nanostructured BCC phase with refined grain sizes that may enhance both ductility and irradiation resistance by reducing defect mean free paths. Nevertheless, the challenge remains to preserve the ultra-high temperature strength of NbMoTaW while ensuring favorable ductility.

directions.direction: Surface modification or coating to mitigate irradiation-induced surface degradation
directions.assessment: Applying a protective coating or surface treatment could locally suppress irradiation-induced blistering or amorphization. While this may improve the surface stability under helium implantation, it does not directly address the intrinsic room-temperature brittleness of the bulk NbMoTaW alloy.

choice.direction: Minor alloying addition of boron to promote intergranular boride precipitation
choice.why: This approach directly addresses both the room-temperature ductility issue and irradiation tolerance by engineering the grain boundaries, a known weak link in BCC refractory HEAs. Literature evidence (e.g., PMC9572892) supports the use of boron to induce beneficial intergranular precipitates that enhance grain-boundary cohesion without sacrificing the single-phase BCC structure needed for high-temperature performance.
